questions.q: What problem does a delta deployment solve?
options: It eliminates the need for Apex tests
It replaces GitHub Actions with a different CI tool
A full deploy sends every component in the source directory on every run, even unchanged ones, which is slow on large orgs -- delta deployments send only what actually changed
It removes the need for authentication
questions.explain: Delta deployments compute exactly which components changed between two commits and deploy only those, avoiding the cost of redeploying everything on every run.

questions.q: What does the sf sgd source delta command actually produce?
options: A compiled binary artifact
A new scratch org
A code coverage report
A package.xml of changed components and a destructiveChanges.xml for deletions/renames, computed between two Git references
questions.explain: SFDX-Git-Delta compares two Git commits and generates exactly these two manifests describing what changed and what was removed.

questions.q: Why does a delta deployment pipeline need actions/checkout@v4 configured with fetch-depth: 0?
options: A default shallow clone only contains the latest commit with no history, and SGD needs full Git history to compute a diff between commits
fetch-depth: 0 speeds up the checkout step with no other effect
fetch-depth: 0 is required to install the Salesforce CLI
It has nothing to do with delta deployments
questions.explain: SGD's diff depends on having the actual prior commits available; a shallow clone (the GitHub Actions default) doesn't include them, so fetch-depth: 0 pulls the full history delta computation needs.

questions.q: Which flag applies a destructive-changes manifest alongside a regular sf project deploy start deployment?
options: --test-level
--dry-run
--coverage-formatters
--post-destructive-changes
questions.explain: --post-destructive-changes points the deploy command at the destructiveChanges.xml SGD generated, so deletions and renames get applied along with the regular additions/modifications.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about the risk of a delta deployment computed against the wrong base commit?
options: There is no risk, delta deployments are always exactly equivalent to a full deploy
Salesforce automatically detects and corrects an incorrect delta
It can produce an incomplete manifest, silently shipping a partial change -- which is exactly why a pipeline should keep a manually-triggerable full-deploy fallback available
The risk only applies to sandbox deployments, never production
questions.explain: A wrong base commit (from a force-push, a confusing merge, an undetected rename) can produce an incomplete delta manifest -- the specific scenario Lesson 6's fallback principle exists to guard against.
